title: He carried a sheep… while we were busy pretending we didn’t need saving.
paragraphs:
He carried a sheep…
while we were busy pretending we didn’t need saving.
Because something in you just flinched.
You’ve learned how to look strong.

Smile right.
Post right.
Serve in church.
Say “I’m okay.”
There’s a quiet ache you don’t talk about.

A hidden pattern.
A private compromise.
A voice that whispers, “If they really knew you…”

You don’t feel lost enough to cry out…
but you’re not free enough to rest.

You don’t need improvement.
You need rescue.
Because Scripture doesn’t describe us as “slightly off.”
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way…” (Isaiah 53:6)

That includes the strong ones.
The leaders.
The ones who know the verses but still feel empty at night.
And sheep don’t wander because they’re rebellious geniuses.
They wander because they’re blind to danger.

Not always loud.
Not always dramatic.

Hidden behind “I deserve this”
or “it’s not that bad.”
But slowly—it separates you from the Shepherd.
Now here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11)
Because a shepherd doesn’t negotiate with wolves.
And here’s the part most people miss:

The greatest danger wasn’t outside the flock.
It was inside your heart.
Your quiet belief that you can manage your own soul.
That you don’t really need saving—just a little help.
But Jesus didn’t come to assist you.
He came to die for you.
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

While you were still hiding.
Still pretending.
Still wandering.
He didn’t wait for your cleanup.

You are more sinful than you admit.
And more loved than you can comprehend.
And both meet at the cross.
“I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me.” (John 10:14)

He knows your name.
Your patterns.
Your shame.
Are you still pretending you’re okay?
Still managing sin instead of surrendering it?
Still standing in the crowd while your soul quietly drifts?
You don’t need to impress the Shepherd.
You need to let Him find you.

It’s dropping the act.
Turning from sin.
Admitting, “I can’t carry myself anymore.”
And trusting the One who already carried the cross.

Not guilt alone—
but a pull.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27)

Bring the secret.
Bring the shame.
Bring the version of you you’ve been protecting.
Because the Shepherd is not looking to expose you.
